papers.title: UMoE:Unlocking Every Expert in Domain-Specific Training
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity without proportional compute cost and have become a key architecture for frontier large language models (LLMs). Yet domain-specific post-training inherits an expert pool shaped by mixed-domain pre-training: a substantial subset of experts contributes little on the target domain, and standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leaves the composition of this pool unchanged. We propose a simple, budget-preserving pipeline that realigns the expert pool to the target domain before fine-tuning. Given a target domain, we (1) prune the experts with lowest domain-aligned saliency, (2) regrow the expert pool to its original size through perturbation-based expert expansion, and (3) apply standard SFT. The resulting model preserves the original expert count, parameter count, and inference cost. With a single frozen recipe and no per-domain hyperparameter tuning, UMoE consistently improves over direct sft across two MoE architectures (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, and agentic coding), and 12 benchmarks. Representative improvements are 3.4 points in math average accuracy, 6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified. On a strong in-house math corpus, direct sft already surpasses Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking (82.81 vs.\ 81.06), yet UMoE further raises the average to 84.17, an additional 1.36 points, demonstrating robustness to a substantially stronger SFT regime. Data-scaling experiments further show that the gain persists as training data grows. Analysis reveals that the direct-SFT model allocates substantial routed-expert compute to a low-saliency subset that can be removed post hoc with little average degradation; UMoE turns this redundant capacity into useful domain capacity and achieves lower training loss, with gains spanning all difficulty levels in downstream evaluation.

summary.takeaway: UMoE reorganizes the expert pool of pretrained MoE LLMs by pruning low-saliency experts and regrowing them via perturbation, yielding consistent domain-specific performance gains without increasing model size or inference cost.
summary.problem: Standard supervised fine-tuning of pretrained MoE models leaves many experts poorly aligned to the target domain, wasting capacity and limiting domain-specific adaptation.
summary.method: UMoE prunes the least domain-salient experts using a calibration set, regrows the expert pool by perturbation-based expansion to restore original size, then applies standard supervised fine-tuning.
summary.evidence: UMoE improves benchmark averages across five domains and two MoE architectures, e.g., +3.4 points math accuracy and +6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified, while preserving parameter count and inference cost.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of UMoE’s impact on inference latency or memory beyond parameter count, nor does it explore alternative pruning ratios or perturbation scales extensively.
summary.why_for_you: UMoE offers an efficient, budget-preserving approach to enhance domain-specific fine-tuning of large MoE LLMs by better utilizing expert capacity, relevant for improving trustworthy and efficient LLM adaptation.

signals.text: UMoE achieves a 3.4-point average accuracy improvement on math benchmarks and a 6.0-point gain on SWE-bench Verified by reorganizing experts before fine-tuning, demonstrating robust domain adaptation across multiple datasets.

The method uses REAP saliency scores on a calibration subset to prune the bottom 50% of experts per layer, then regenerates pruned experts by copying and symmetrically perturbing surviving experts’ MLP weights and router rows.

Analysis shows direct supervised fine-tuning routes substantial compute to low-saliency experts that can be pruned with minimal degradation, whereas UMoE reallocates this capacity to domain-aligned experts, reducing training loss and improving downstream performance.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the inefficiency in domain-specific fine-tuning of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, where many experts pretrained on mixed domains contribute little to the target domain. The authors propose UMoE, a three-step pipeline that first prunes experts with the lowest domain-aligned saliency using a calibration dataset, then regrows the expert pool to its original size by perturbation-based expansion of surviving experts, and finally applies standard supervised fine-tuning. This preserves the original model architecture, parameter count, and inference cost, ensuring deployment budget consistency. Evaluations on two MoE architectures (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) across five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, agentic coding) and 12 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, including a 3.4-point gain in math accuracy and 6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified. The approach is robust to stronger fine-tuning regimes and scales well with training data size. The key insight is that direct fine-tuning wastes capacity on low-saliency experts, whereas UMoE reallocates this capacity to domain-relevant experts, improving training efficiency and downstream task performance.

methodology.title: Domain-Aligned Expert Pruning
methodology.detail: UMoE scores each expert’s domain relevance using REAP saliency on a calibration subset of the target domain data, combining router gate values and activation norms. It prunes the bottom 50% of experts per layer, retaining those most relevant to the domain to form a domain-aligned expert subset.

methodology.title: Budget-Preserving Expert Expansion
methodology.detail: To restore the original expert count, each pruned slot is reinitialized by copying MLP weights and router rows from surviving experts in a round-robin fashion. Both the parent and regrown experts are independently perturbed with Gaussian noise scaled by parameter standard deviation (σ=0.05) to promote specialization and avoid initialization asymmetry.

methodology.title: Standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
methodology.detail: After expert pool reorganization, the model undergoes standard supervised fine-tuning on the full domain-specific dataset using cross-entropy loss. This step updates the domain-aligned experts to improve downstream task performance without changing model size or inference cost.

methodology.title: Evaluation Across Architectures and Domains
methodology.detail: UMoE is evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE architectures across five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, agentic coding) using multiple benchmarks and varying SFT data scales to validate generality and robustness.

mechanism.title: Domain-Aligned Saliency Scoring
mechanism.detail: Experts are scored by REAP saliency, which integrates router gate weights and activation norms over a calibration set, reflecting each expert’s functional importance under the target domain distribution. This guides pruning decisions to retain domain-relevant experts.

mechanism.title: Symmetric Perturbation for Expert Expansion
mechanism.detail: Copied experts are perturbed symmetrically on both the parent and regrown copies by adding Gaussian noise scaled by parameter standard deviation, applied to both MLP weights and router rows. This symmetric perturbation avoids initialization bias and encourages functional specialization.

mechanism.title: Fixed Budget Constraint
mechanism.detail: UMoE maintains the original expert count E and active expert count K, preserving parameter count and inference cost. This ensures that domain adaptation does not increase deployment resource requirements.

experiments.title: Domain-Specific Fine-Tuning on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
experiments.detail: UMoE is tested on two MoE architectures with 128 and 256 routed experts respectively, across five domains with domain-specific SFT datasets and multiple benchmarks, including math competitions (AIME, HMMT), code reasoning (LiveCodeBench), science (GPQA-Diamond), tool-use (τ-bench), and agentic coding (SWE-bench Verified).

experiments.title: Data-Scaling Experiments
experiments.detail: UMoE’s performance gains persist across varying amounts of supervised fine-tuning data, demonstrating robustness to training data scale and confirming that improvements are not limited to small data regimes.

experiments.title: Ablation on Saliency Metrics and Perturbation Design
experiments.detail: Comparisons among REAP saliency, activation frequency, and Expert Activation Norm (EAN) show REAP and frequency are competitive, with EAN weaker. Perturbing both parent and regrown experts symmetrically outperforms one-sided perturbation, and perturbing both router and MLP weights yields complementary benefits.

findings.title: UMoE Improves Domain-Specific Accuracy
findings.detail: UMoE consistently outperforms direct supervised fine-tuning, e.g., raising math average accuracy by 3.4 points and SWE-bench Verified pass@1 by 6.0 points, demonstrating effective domain adaptation.

findings.title: Robustness to Stronger Fine-Tuning Regimes
findings.detail: On a strong in-house math corpus where direct SFT already surpasses a strong baseline (82.81 vs. 81.06), UMoE further improves average accuracy to 84.17, showing gains under stronger SFT conditions.

findings.title: Expert Pool Reorganization Reduces Redundancy
findings.detail: Direct SFT routes substantial compute to low-saliency experts that can be pruned post hoc with little degradation, whereas UMoE reallocates this capacity to domain-aligned experts, lowering training loss and improving performance across difficulty levels.

findings.title: Perturbation Design is Critical
findings.detail: Symmetric perturbation of both parent and regrown experts on MLP and router parameters is essential; one-sided perturbation leads to routing decline and performance degradation.

contributions: Proposed UMoE, a domain-aware expert pool reorganization method that prunes and regrows experts to improve domain-specific fine-tuning without increasing model size or inference cost.
Introduced a budget-preserving expert expansion technique using symmetric perturbation of copied experts to promote specialization.
Demonstrated consistent performance gains across multiple MoE architectures, five diverse domains, and 12 benchmarks, including strong math and agentic coding tasks.
Provided analysis showing that direct fine-tuning wastes capacity on low-saliency experts, which UMoE effectively reallocates to domain-relevant experts.
Validated robustness of UMoE gains across varying supervised fine-tuning data scales and stronger fine-tuning regimes.
limitations: The impact of UMoE on inference latency and memory usage beyond parameter count is not analyzed.
The pruning ratio is fixed at 50% without extensive exploration of alternative ratios or adaptive pruning strategies.
The perturbation scale σ is fixed at 0.05; sensitivity to this hyperparameter is not deeply studied.
UMoE relies on a calibration subset for saliency scoring, but the effect of calibration set size and representativeness is not detailed.
open_questions: How does UMoE affect inference efficiency metrics such as latency and memory footprint in deployment scenarios?
Can adaptive or dynamic pruning ratios based on domain complexity further improve expert pool reorganization?
What is the sensitivity of UMoE performance to the choice and size of the calibration dataset used for saliency scoring?
Could alternative perturbation schemes or learned expert regeneration methods yield better specialization and downstream gains?

papers.title: DT-Guard: Intent-Driven Reasoning-Active Training for Reasoning-Free LLM Safety Guardrail
papers.abstract: Large language models deployed in open-world applications require safety guardrails that are both robust to complex risks and efficient enough for low-latency runtime moderation. Existing guardrails face a practical trade-off between lightweight classification-based models, which are efficient but often struggle with concealed intent, ambiguous semantics, and borderline safety decisions, and reasoning-based guards, which improve judgment quality but introduce additional token generation and inference latency. We present DT-Guard, a content safety guardrail model based on a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm. The key idea is to use reasoning supervision during training while emitting only structured safety labels at inference time. DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process, Intent - Category - Safety, and constructs an intent-driven dataset with intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. To further improve hard-case robustness, we propose Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO), which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable samples, and applies targeted supervised and preference optimization accordingly. At inference time, DT-Guard directly generates structured labels without explicit reasoning traces, preserving deployment efficiency. Experiments on prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks show that DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870, respectively. With only a 4B backbone, it reaches a dual-side average F1 of 0.878, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines. These results demonstrate that reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into low-latency safety discrimination.

summary.takeaway: DT-Guard internalizes reasoning supervision during training to achieve efficient, reasoning-free inference for robust LLM safety guardrails.
summary.problem: Existing LLM safety guardrails trade off between efficient but shallow classification and robust but slow reasoning-based methods.
summary.method: DT-Guard uses a progressive Intent → Category → Safety decision process with reasoning-active training and rollout-guided hard-case optimization, emitting only structured labels at inference.
summary.evidence: DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 on prompt-side and 0.870 on response-side benchmarks, outperforming 8B baselines with a 4B backbone.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of failure modes or generalization beyond tested benchmarks.
summary.why_for_you: DT-Guard offers a novel training paradigm that leverages reasoning supervision to improve adversarial robustness and efficiency in LLM safety guardrails.

signals.text: DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process: Intent recognition, risk Category attribution, and final Safety prediction, enabling clearer intermediate supervision for complex cases.

Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO) stratifies samples by multi-rollout consistency into mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable, applying targeted supervised fine-tuning and contrastive preference optimization.
Selective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training on borderline samples improves average F1 from 0.828 (full CoT) to 0.860, showing that uniform CoT supervision mismatches reasoning-free inference.

deep_dive.overview: DT-Guard addresses the challenge of deploying LLM safety guardrails that are both robust to complex, concealed intents and efficient for low-latency inference. Existing methods either rely on lightweight classification models that struggle with ambiguous or adversarial inputs or on reasoning-based models that incur high inference latency due to token generation of reasoning chains. DT-Guard introduces a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm, where explicit reasoning supervision is used only during training to internalize complex safety judgments. The model predicts structured safety labels through a progressive decision process: identifying user intent, attributing risk categories, and adjudicating safety levels. To enhance robustness on hard cases, DT-Guard employs RG-PHO, which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify sample difficulty and applies tailored supervised and preference-based optimization. Experiments on multiple prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks demonstrate that DT-Guard outperforms larger 8B parameter baselines with only a 4B backbone, achieving average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870 respectively, validating the effectiveness of reasoning supervision internalization for efficient safety discrimination.

methodology.title: Intent-Driven Progressive Safety Judgment
methodology.detail: Safety judgment is decomposed into a three-stage process: Intent recognition to capture underlying user motivation, Category attribution to assign relevant risk types, and Safety prediction to determine final safety labels. This structured approach provides intermediate supervision signals that improve robustness on ambiguous and borderline cases.

methodology.title: Reasoning-Active Training with Reasoning-Free Inference
methodology.detail: During training, DT-Guard uses explicit reasoning trajectories as supervision to guide the model in understanding complex safety decisions. At inference, the model emits only structured safety labels without generating reasoning chains, preserving low-latency deployment.

methodology.title: Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO)
methodology.detail: RG-PHO uses multiple model rollouts to assess sample consistency, stratifying samples into stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable. Persistently failed samples receive stronger supervised fine-tuning, while preference-unstable samples undergo contrastive preference optimization to stabilize judgments.

methodology.title: Selective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Supervision
methodology.detail: CoT reasoning supervision is selectively applied only to borderline samples rather than uniformly across all data, mitigating format mismatch with reasoning-free inference and improving overall F1 performance.

mechanism.title: No explicit mechanism equations provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but describes the progressive decision process and rollout consistency as conceptual mechanisms for improving safety judgment robustness.

experiments.title: Benchmark Evaluation on Prompt-Side and Response-Side Safety
experiments.detail: DT-Guard is evaluated on 10 prompt-side benchmarks (e.g., ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation, AegisSafety) and 7 response-side benchmarks (e.g., HarmBench-Response, SafeRLHF). Metrics reported are classification F1 scores, comparing against Qwen3Guard and YuFeng-XGuard baselines with parameter sizes from 0.6B to 8B.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies on Training Components
experiments.detail: Ablations isolate the effects of intent labels, CoT allocation strategies, hard-case supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO). Selective CoT on borderline samples yields the best average F1, confirming the importance of matching supervision to sample difficulty.

experiments.title: Model Size and Efficiency Comparison
experiments.detail: DT-Guard with a 4B backbone outperforms strong 8B guardrail baselines, demonstrating that reasoning supervision internalized during training can compensate for smaller model size while maintaining low-latency inference.

findings.title: Superior Safety Classification Performance
findings.detail: DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 on prompt-side and 0.870 on response-side safety benchmarks, outperforming Qwen3Guard-8B (0.852 prompt-side) and YuFeng-XGuard-8B baselines.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Intent Labels
findings.detail: Adding intent supervision improves prompt-side average F1 from 0.855 to 0.863, indicating that modeling interaction motivation aids in disambiguating semantically similar but safety-divergent requests.

findings.title: Selective CoT Training Improves Robustness
findings.detail: Applying chain-of-thought supervision only to borderline samples increases average F1 to 0.860, whereas full CoT training reduces performance to 0.828 due to format mismatch with reasoning-free inference.

findings.title: RG-PHO Enhances Hard-Case Handling
findings.detail: Multi-rollout consistency stratification enables targeted optimization of persistently failed and preference-unstable samples, improving model stability and judgment quality on difficult cases.

findings.title: Efficiency Gains from Reasoning-Free Inference
findings.detail: By emitting only structured safety labels at inference, DT-Guard avoids token-generation overhead of reasoning chains, enabling deployment in low-latency, high-throughput industrial systems.

contributions: Proposed DT-Guard, a safety guardrail model combining reasoning-active training with reasoning-free inference for efficient and robust safety judgment.
Formulated safety judgment as a progressive Intent → Category → Safety decision process with intent-driven dataset construction.
Introduced Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization to stratify and optimize hard safety cases via multi-rollout consistency.
Demonstrated that reasoning supervision can be internalized to outperform larger guardrail models with smaller backbones under low-latency inference constraints.
limitations: Lack of detailed failure mode analysis or error case studies limits understanding of residual risks.
Generalization to unseen or evolving safety risks beyond benchmark datasets is not evaluated.
No explicit mechanism or theoretical guarantees are provided for the rollout consistency stratification approach.
The impact of model architecture variations or larger-scale training data on DT-Guard performance is not explored.
open_questions: How well does DT-Guard generalize to novel or adversarially crafted safety risks outside the training distribution?
Can rollout-guided hard-case optimization be extended or formalized with theoretical guarantees for safety-critical applications?
What are the trade-offs between reasoning supervision granularity and inference efficiency in other safety-critical LLM tasks?
How does DT-Guard perform when integrated with larger backbone models or multimodal inputs?

papers.title: UltraX: Refining Pre-Training Data at Scale with Adaptive Programmatic Editing
papers.abstract: As available training data approaches its physical limit, gains from Scaling Laws have begun to diminish. Consequently, improving Large Language Models (LLMs) now depends less on data expansion and more on higher-quality data utilization. However, in the context of large-scale corpora, existing refinement methodologies face significant limitations in quality, efficiency, and reliability: Rule-based approaches are constrained by fixed heuristics and struggle with instance-level variations; LLM-based approaches improve quality but fail to meet the efficiency and reliability requirements of large-scale data processing. To address these challenges, we propose UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework for large-scale pre-training data that completes the editing function space by introducing insertion in addition to deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level editing. Specifically, UltraX builds a reliable program-supervision generation pipeline. In this pipeline, dataset-adaptive prompt optimization first guides an expert LLM to produce high-quality end-to-end refined texts, and Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement then convert original-refined text pairs into structured program supervision. Meanwhile, UltraX improves supervision quality and stabilizes the training distribution with low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination. During inference and execution, it normalizes and validates model outputs through sliding-window prediction, global operation aggregation, and systematic post-processing, improving the stability and reliability of large-scale execution. Experiments show that UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all corpora and also matches or surpasses baselines with fewer training tokens, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability.

summary.takeaway: UltraX introduces a function-calling refinement framework with insertion, deletion, and modification operations, achieving superior data refinement quality and efficiency for large-scale LLM pre-training.
summary.problem: Existing large-scale pre-training data refinement methods either lack fine-grained editing capabilities or fail to scale efficiently and reliably to massive corpora.
summary.method: UltraX constructs a program-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, dynamic context replacement, and robust execution with sliding-window prediction and post-processing.
summary.evidence: Experiments with 1B parameter models pretrained on multiple corpora show UltraX surpasses baselines by over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets while using fewer training tokens.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of UltraX’s performance on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation nor does it address potential biases inherited from expert LLMs used in supervision generation.
summary.why_for_you: UltraX offers a scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement approach that improves pre-training data quality and efficiency, directly addressing challenges in trustworthy and efficient LLM data utilization.

signals.text: UltraX achieves over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets in downstream tasks using 1B parameter models pretrained from scratch, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability compared to baselines.

UltraX’s program-supervision pipeline includes dataset-adaptive prompt optimization guiding an expert LLM to generate high-quality refined texts, followed by line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement to convert text pairs into structured editing programs.

UltraX stabilizes training distribution and improves supervision quality via low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination, while inference uses sliding-window prediction and global operation aggregation to ensure stable large-scale execution.

deep_dive.overview: UltraX addresses the diminishing returns of scaling LLM training data by focusing on improving data quality through fine-grained, programmatic editing of pre-training corpora. Unlike prior rule-based or LLM-based refinement methods limited by fixed heuristics or computational inefficiency, UltraX completes the editing function space by adding insertion to deletion and modification, enabling nuanced instance-level edits. It constructs a reliable program supervision pipeline where an expert LLM, guided by dataset-adaptive prompts, produces end-to-end refined texts. These are converted into structured editing operations via line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement. To ensure training stability and quality, UltraX filters low-confidence examples and controls sampling ratios of operation types. During inference, it segments long documents with sliding windows, predicts local operations, aggregates them globally, and applies systematic post-processing to produce stable, executable refinement programs. Experiments with 1B models pretrained on multiple corpora demonstrate UltraX’s superior average performance and data efficiency, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on several datasets, validating its approach to scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement for LLM pre-training.

methodology.title: Dataset-Adaptive Prompt Optimization
methodology.detail: UltraX first optimizes prompts tailored to each dataset to guide an expert LLM in generating high-quality, end-to-end refined texts from raw inputs, ensuring that the refinement captures dataset-specific nuances and semantic improvements.

methodology.title: Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement
methodology.detail: These techniques convert original and refined text pairs into structured program supervision by aligning lines between versions and replacing context dynamically, enabling the extraction of precise editing operations such as insertion, deletion, and modification.

methodology.title: Low-Confidence Example Filtering and Ratio-Controlled Sampling
methodology.detail: To improve supervision quality and stabilize training, UltraX filters out examples with low confidence scores and controls the sampling ratio of different operation combinations, balancing the training distribution across insertion, deletion, and modification operations.

methodology.title: Sliding-Window Segment-wise Operation Prediction
methodology.detail: During inference, UltraX segments long documents using a sliding-window approach, normalizes line numbers, and independently predicts editing operation sequences for each segment to handle length constraints and maintain local context.

methodology.title: Global Operation Aggregation and Systematic Post-Processing
methodology.detail: Local operation sequences from segments are merged into a global program by mapping operations to global line numbers, filtering duplicates, merging adjacent or interfering operations, and applying fallback mechanisms to ensure stable, executable refinement programs.

mechanism.title: Programmatic Editing with Complete Operation Space
mechanism.detail: UltraX extends the editing function space by including insertion alongside deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level edits that preserve semantic coherence and restore missing information, overcoming limitations of prior deletion-only or replacement-only frameworks.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Theoretical Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but describes a deterministic function executor that applies predicted editing operations to original texts, ensuring auditable and interpretable refinement.

experiments.title: Pretraining 1B Parameter Models on Multiple Corpora
experiments.detail: UltraX was evaluated by pretraining 1B parameter language models from scratch on multiple large-scale corpora, comparing downstream task performance against baselines including raw data and ProX refinement, measuring average accuracy improvements and data efficiency.

experiments.title: Downstream Task Evaluation Across Ten Tasks
experiments.detail: Performance was assessed on ten downstream tasks including ARC-C, ARC-E, CSQA, HellaS, MMLU, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoG, and SciQ, with varying numbers of training tokens, demonstrating consistent gains and surpassing baselines with fewer tokens.

experiments.title: Ablation on Operation Combination Sampling
experiments.detail: The effect of ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination was analyzed to understand its impact on training stability and refinement quality, showing that balanced sampling improves model performance.

findings.title: Superior Average Performance
findings.detail: UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all evaluated corpora, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on multiple datasets compared to baseline methods.

findings.title: Improved Data Efficiency
findings.detail: UltraX matches or surpasses baseline refinement methods while using fewer training tokens, indicating stronger data efficiency in pre-training.

findings.title: Fine-Grained Refinement Balances Noise Removal and Preservation
findings.detail: Analyses suggest UltraX’s inclusion of insertion operations alongside deletion and modification enables better balance between removing noise and preserving useful information, reducing semantic fragmentation.

findings.title: Stable Large-Scale Execution
findings.detail: The sliding-window prediction, global aggregation, and systematic post-processing pipeline improve the stability and reliability of large-scale data refinement execution.

contributions: Proposed UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework introducing insertion to complete the editing function space for fine-grained instance-level editing.
Developed a reliable seed-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, and dynamic context replacement to generate structured program supervision.
Designed a robust large-scale execution pipeline with systematic post-processing to handle duplicate matching, ambiguous replacements, and operation interference.
Demonstrated consistent downstream performance improvements and stronger data efficiency across multiple large-scale pre-training corpora.
limitations: Lack of detailed evaluation on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation and its impact on refinement quality.
Potential biases and errors inherited from expert LLMs used in generating seed supervision are not explicitly analyzed.
No formal theoretical or causal mechanism is provided to explain the editing operation interactions or their effect on model performance.
Limited discussion on the computational cost and scalability trade-offs compared to other LLM-based refinement methods.
open_questions: How does UltraX perform on extremely long documents or streaming data beyond the sliding-window segmentation approach?
What are the effects of expert LLM biases on the quality and reliability of generated program supervision?
Can the programmatic editing framework be extended to incorporate semantic or syntactic constraints to further improve refinement quality?
How does UltraX compare in computational efficiency and cost to other state-of-the-art LLM-based refinement methods at larger model scales?

papers.title: HyperSafe: Inference-Time Safety Recovery for Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models can be fragile under fine-tuning, as even benign task adaptation may increase harmful compliance. Existing defenses mainly follow two directions: they either intervene during or after fine-tuning through retraining or weight modification, which can be costly and may hurt task performance, or they use model-agnostic safety classifiers, which may miss failures specific to a given fine-tuned checkpoint. These limitations motivate a post hoc, model-specific, and non-invasive approach to safety restoration. To meet these requirements, we propose HyperSafe, a framework that restores safety behavior by generating a model-specific Safe Side Network (SSN) for each fine-tuned checkpoint. HyperSafe uses layer-wise activation fingerprints to capture how fine-tuning changes the model's inner representations. With a small set of given calibration prompts, the hypernetwork maps these fingerprints to the parameters of the \ssn{} in a single forward pass. The generated \ssn{} runs alongside the frozen fine-tuned model and performs prompt-level safety classification: harmful prompts are routed to refusal, while safe prompts are answered by the original fine-tuned model. Thus, HyperSafe requires no gradient updates, no safety data at deployment time, and no modification to the deployed model weights. We evaluate HyperSafe on two model families, Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B, across multiple safety benchmarks. HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19-31% to below 1% on every held-out checkpoint, while keeping downstream task accuracy within 1% of the fine-tuned baseline on average. Code is available at https://github.com/nokronim/project-safety-remedy.

summary.takeaway: HyperSafe generates model-specific Safe Side Networks at inference time to restore safety in fine-tuned LLMs, reducing harmful outputs below 1% while preserving task accuracy within 1%.
summary.problem: Fine-tuning safety-aligned large language models often degrades their safety alignment, increasing harmful response rates significantly.
summary.method: HyperSafe uses layer-wise activation fingerprints from calibration prompts to generate a Safe Side Network via a hypernetwork that classifies prompts at inference, routing harmful ones to refusal without modifying model weights.
summary.evidence: Evaluations on Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B across multiple safety benchmarks show HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% to below 1% on all held-out checkpoints while maintaining task accuracy within 1% of fine-tuned baselines.
summary.limitations: The method relies on a calibration set and may degrade if instruction-following data is excluded; it has been evaluated primarily on LoRA fine-tuned checkpoints and two model families.
summary.why_for_you: HyperSafe offers a non-invasive, model-specific, and efficient inference-time safety recovery approach that preserves downstream task performance, addressing fine-tuning-induced safety degradation without retraining or weight modification.

signals.text: HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% in LoRA fine-tuned Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B models to below 1% across 12 held-out datasets, demonstrating strong zero-shot safety generalization.

The Safe Side Network (SSN) is generated by a hypernetwork that maps layer-wise activation fingerprints from a small calibration prompt set to SSN parameters in a single forward pass, enabling prompt-level safety classification without weight updates.

Ablation studies show removing safe-probe supervision or domain-specific calibration degrades task accuracy and safety, indicating the importance of functional supervision and diverse calibration data for SSN effectiveness.

deep_dive.overview: Fine-tuning aligned large language models often compromises their safety, increasing harmful outputs despite benign task adaptation. Existing defenses either intervene during fine-tuning with costly constraints, modify model weights post hoc risking task performance degradation, or use model-agnostic classifiers that miss fine-tuning-specific failures. HyperSafe addresses these limitations by generating a model-specific Safe Side Network (SSN) at inference time using a hypernetwork conditioned on layer-wise activation fingerprints extracted from a small calibration prompt set. The SSN runs alongside the frozen fine-tuned model, classifying prompts as harmful or safe and routing harmful prompts to refusal, thus restoring safety without retraining or weight modification. Evaluations on Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B across multiple safety benchmarks demonstrate that HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% to below 1% while preserving task accuracy within 1%. Ablations confirm the necessity of functional supervision and calibration diversity. This approach enables deployment of fine-tuned models with restored safety guarantees efficiently and non-invasively.

methodology.title: Layer-wise Activation Fingerprints
methodology.detail: Extracts activation patterns from multiple layers of the fine-tuned model using a small set of calibration prompts to capture fine-tuning-induced representation changes, serving as input to the hypernetwork.

methodology.title: Hypernetwork Parameter Generation
methodology.detail: A hypernetwork maps the extracted activation fingerprints to the parameters of the Safe Side Network in a single forward pass, enabling rapid generation of a model-specific safety classifier without gradient updates.

methodology.title: Safe Side Network (SSN) Architecture
methodology.detail: The SSN is a lightweight classifier with 12 side layers and reduced hidden size (h/4) that runs alongside the frozen fine-tuned model, performing prompt-level safety classification to route harmful prompts to refusal.

methodology.title: Prompt-level Safety Classification
methodology.detail: The SSN classifies each input prompt as harmful or safe; harmful prompts are refused, while safe prompts are answered by the original fine-tuned model, preserving task utility.

methodology.title: Training Objective and Calibration
methodology.detail: The hypernetwork and SSN are trained using a combination of functional supervision losses including safe-probe supervision and domain calibration prompts, ensuring discriminative safety classification and minimal over-blocking.

mechanism.title: No explicit mechanism equations provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or causal models but explains that layer-wise activation fingerprints capture fine-tuning changes, which the hypernetwork uses to generate SSN parameters for prompt-level safety classification.

experiments.title: Model Families and Fine-tuning
experiments.detail: Evaluations conducted on Qwen2-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct models fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 16, α=32) across 22 diverse datasets spanning QA, reasoning, math, classification, code, and instruction-following.

experiments.title: Safety Benchmarks and Evaluation Protocol
experiments.detail: Safety evaluated on BeaverTails (700 prompts, 14 categories), AdvBench (520 prompts), and HEx-PHI (330 prompts, 11 categories) with disjoint training and evaluation splits; harmful rate and task accuracy metrics reported.

experiments.title: Comparison Baselines
experiments.detail: Compared against base aligned models, LoRA fine-tuned models without safety mechanisms, and Llama Guard 4 (12B) external classifier, demonstrating superior safety reduction and task accuracy preservation.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Ablations on LLaMA-3-8B show removing safe-probe supervision or domain calibration degrades accuracy and safety; calibration prompt set size impacts fingerprint quality and SSN performance; SSNs trained on LoRA checkpoints transfer to full fine-tuning.

findings.title: Safety Restoration
findings.detail: HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% in fine-tuned models to below 1% across all held-out datasets and model families, achieving over 95% relative reduction in harmful outputs.

findings.title: Task Accuracy Preservation
findings.detail: Task accuracy remains within 1 percentage point of the fine-tuned baseline on average, indicating minimal utility loss despite safety restoration.

findings.title: Generalization and Transfer
findings.detail: SSNs generated from LoRA fingerprints transfer unchanged to fully fine-tuned counterparts, maintaining harmful rates ≤0.1% and stable task accuracy.

findings.title: Calibration Data Importance
findings.detail: Instruction-following calibration data is critical for safety; removing it substantially increases harmful rates, while removing other categories has minimal effect.

findings.title: Efficiency
findings.detail: SSN adds only 3–4% of backbone parameters and requires a single hypernetwork forward pass amortized over prompts; safe prompts bypass SSN during decoding, keeping generation cost unchanged.

contributions: Proposed HyperSafe, a novel inference-time safety recovery framework generating model-specific Safe Side Networks without weight modification or retraining.
Introduced layer-wise activation fingerprints as a representation of fine-tuning changes for hypernetwork conditioning.
Demonstrated strong safety restoration reducing harmful outputs below 1% while preserving task accuracy within 1% across two large LLM families and multiple safety benchmarks.
Provided extensive ablations showing the importance of functional supervision, calibration diversity, and prompt set size.
Showed SSN transferability from LoRA to full fine-tuning, enabling practical deployment without re-alignment.
limitations: Dependence on a sufficiently diverse and representative calibration prompt set, especially instruction-following data, for effective safety classification.
Evaluations limited to two model families (Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B) and LoRA fine-tuning; generalization to other architectures or fine-tuning methods is unverified.
No explicit theoretical mechanism or formal guarantees provided for safety restoration effectiveness.
Potential residual harmful outputs remain (up to 0.7% in some datasets), indicating non-zero failure risk.
open_questions: How well does HyperSafe generalize to other fine-tuning methods beyond LoRA and to larger or different LLM architectures?
Can the calibration prompt set be optimized or minimized further without degrading safety and accuracy?
What are the theoretical limits and guarantees of safety restoration achievable by model-specific SSNs generated from activation fingerprints?
How does HyperSafe perform against adaptive adversarial harmful prompts designed to evade the SSN?

papers.title: WordVoice: Explicit and Decoupled Multi-Dimensional Word-Level Control for LLM-Based TTS
papers.abstract: While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems have achieved remarkable naturalness, they predominantly rely on implicit end-to-end generation paradigms, resulting in coarse-grained control. In scenarios demanding precise stylistic interventions and strict temporal alignment, such as audiobook narration and video dubbing, the inability to explicitly manipulate word-level acoustic attributes remains a critical bottleneck. This limitation is primarily amplified by the severe scarcity of fine-grained annotated datasets and the architectural challenge of integrating multi-dimensional control signals into discrete autoregressive generation. To address this, we propose a unified framework for highly precise word-level control. First, we construct WordVoice-5A, a massive 4.7k-hour bilingual dataset featuring five-dimensional word-level annotations (duration, boundary, energy, pitch and tone) developed through a rigorous linguistically-guided pipeline. Second, we introduce WordVoice to transform the implicit generation process into an explicit, highly controllable paradigm. Specifically, we introduce a bound-token mechanism within the LLM to formulate an explicit ``acoustic planning'' process, enabling adaptive multi-task prosodic planning and flexible manual intervention. Furthermore, we augment the token-to-waveform stage with a fine-grained acoustic modulation module, bridging the resolution gap to strictly align word-level attributes between highly compressed discrete tokens and continuous waveforms. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WordVoice achieves superior, decoupled control over multiple acoustic dimensions while maintaining competitive zero-shot synthesis stability. The code and audio samples are publicly available at https://xxh333.github.io/wordvoice-demo/.

summary.takeaway: WordVoice introduces explicit, multi-dimensional word-level control in LLM-based TTS, achieving precise prosodic manipulation and strict temporal alignment.
summary.problem: Current LLM-based TTS systems lack fine-grained, explicit control over multiple acoustic attributes at the word level, limiting applications requiring precise stylistic and temporal adjustments.
summary.method: WordVoice combines a large-scale, linguistically annotated dataset (WordVoice-5A) with an explicit bound-token acoustic planning mechanism in the LLM and a fine-grained acoustic modulation module in the token-to-waveform stage.
summary.evidence: Experiments on a 4.7k-hour bilingual test set show WordVoice outperforms baselines like CosyVoice3 in controllability (Ctrl-MOS) and naturalness (N-MOS), with objective metrics confirming superior multi-attribute alignment and temporal precision.
summary.limitations: Tone control remains partially entangled with other acoustic features due to its dynamic nature, and strong localized prosodic variations slightly reduce speaker similarity.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a novel, data-driven framework and architectural design enabling explicit, decoupled multi-dimensional word-level control in LLM-based TTS, advancing trustworthy and precise prosodic synthesis.

signals.text: WordVoice-5A is a 4.7k-hour bilingual dataset with five-dimensional word-level annotations (duration, boundary, energy, pitch, tone), enabling supervised training for explicit multi-attribute control.

The bound-token mechanism restructures the LLM’s autoregressive generation to explicitly plan acoustic attributes before speech token generation, allowing adaptive multi-task prosodic planning and manual intervention.
Objective evaluations show WordVoice reduces duration mean absolute error (Dur-MAE) and boundary error rate (Bnd-ER) compared to MagicTTS, demonstrating improved temporal alignment precision.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical limitation of coarse-grained control in current LLM-based TTS systems by proposing WordVoice, a framework enabling explicit, multi-dimensional word-level control. The authors first construct WordVoice-5A, a large-scale bilingual dataset with detailed word-level acoustic annotations across five dimensions. Leveraging this data, WordVoice introduces a novel bound-token mechanism within the LLM to explicitly plan acoustic attributes in an autoregressive manner, enabling both autonomous prosodic generation and manual attribute specification. To bridge the resolution gap between discrete tokens and continuous waveforms, a fine-grained acoustic modulation module is integrated into the token-to-waveform stage. Extensive experiments on unseen Chinese and English utterances demonstrate that WordVoice achieves superior controllability and naturalness compared to strong baselines, validated by subjective MOS tests and objective acoustic metrics. Ablation studies confirm the decoupling of acoustic attributes and the necessity of the modulation module for detailed acoustic reconstruction. The work significantly advances precise prosodic control in TTS, crucial for applications like audiobook narration and video dubbing requiring strict temporal and stylistic fidelity.

methodology.title: WordVoice-5A Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: A linguistically-guided annotation pipeline produces a 4.7k-hour bilingual dataset with five word-level acoustic attributes: duration, boundary, energy, pitch, and tone. This dataset supports supervised training for explicit multi-dimensional control.

methodology.title: Bound-Token Acoustic Planning Mechanism
methodology.detail: Within the autoregressive LLM, special bound-tokens explicitly represent acoustic attributes, enabling the model to plan prosody before generating speech tokens. This restructures generation from implicit to explicit, allowing adaptive multi-task control and manual intervention.

methodology.title: Fine-Grained Acoustic Modulation Module
methodology.detail: Inserted in the token-to-waveform stage, this module compensates for acoustic details lost during discrete token quantization by modulating continuous waveforms with word-level style tokens, ensuring strict alignment of acoustic attributes.

methodology.title: Training Objectives
methodology.detail: The LLM is trained to predict acoustic attributes and speech tokens autoregressively, while the modulation module uses a Flow Matching objective to reconstruct acoustic details, with random masking of speech tokens to enforce reliance on style conditions.

mechanism.title: Acoustic Planning via Bound-Tokens
mechanism.detail: The bound-token mechanism explicitly encodes word-level acoustic attributes within the LLM’s autoregressive generation, enabling causal reasoning about prosodic execution prior to speech token generation. This explicit planning contrasts with implicit end-to-end generation, facilitating decoupled multi-dimensional control.

mechanism.title: No Additional Mechanistic Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide explicit equations or causal models beyond the description of the bound-token mechanism and Flow Matching loss.

experiments.title: Subjective Evaluation on WordVoice-5A Test Set
experiments.detail: Crowd-sourced listening tests with 20 participants rated 80 utterances per model on naturalness (N-MOS), speaker similarity (Spk-MOS), and word style control (Ctrl-MOS). WordVoice-Control achieved statistically significant improvements in controllability and naturalness over CosyVoice3.

experiments.title: Objective Acoustic Attribute Evaluation
experiments.detail: Metrics such as Word Error Rate (WER), Duration Mean Absolute Error (Dur-MAE), Energy MAE, Pitch MAE, Boundary Error Rate (Bnd-ER), and Tone Relative Error Rate (Ton-RER) were computed on Chinese and English test sets, showing WordVoice variants outperform baselines and ablations.

experiments.title: Temporal Control Precision Comparison
experiments.detail: WordVoice demonstrated lower Dur-MAE and Bnd-ER than MagicTTS variants on both Chinese and English test sets, confirming superior explicit temporal alignment.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies on Attribute Decoupling and Modulation Module
experiments.detail: Single-attribute control experiments confirmed decoupling of duration, boundary, energy, and pitch, with tone showing partial entanglement. Removing the modulation module degraded energy and pitch reconstruction, validating its role in acoustic detail compensation.

findings.title: Superior Multi-Dimensional Control
findings.detail: WordVoice achieves explicit, decoupled control over duration, boundary, energy, pitch, and tone at the word level, outperforming prior methods limited to unidimensional or implicit control.

findings.title: Improved Naturalness and Controllability
findings.detail: WordVoice-Control variant significantly improves naturalness (N-MOS) and word-level style control (Ctrl-MOS) over CosyVoice3, with p<0.05 and p<0.01 respectively, demonstrating effective prosodic planning.

findings.title: Tradeoff in Speaker Similarity
findings.detail: Localized prosodic variations introduced by WordVoice cause minor reductions in speaker similarity (Spk-MOS), reflecting a tradeoff between expressiveness and timbre consistency.

findings.title: Temporal Alignment Precision
findings.detail: WordVoice reduces duration MAE and boundary error rates compared to MagicTTS, confirming more precise explicit temporal control.

findings.title: Necessity of Acoustic Modulation Module
findings.detail: Ablations show that removing the WordVoice-FM module significantly degrades energy and pitch reconstruction, confirming its critical role in restoring acoustic details lost in token quantization.

contributions: Construction and open-sourcing of WordVoice-5A, a large-scale bilingual dataset with five-dimensional word-level acoustic annotations.
Introduction of the bound-token mechanism enabling explicit acoustic planning within an autoregressive LLM for multi-dimensional prosodic control.
Development of a fine-grained acoustic modulation module bridging discrete token representations and continuous waveform synthesis.
Comprehensive evaluation demonstrating superior word-level control, naturalness, and temporal alignment over state-of-the-art baselines.
limitations: Tone attribute control is only partially decoupled due to its dynamic variation nature, complicating absolute disentanglement from other acoustic features.
Strong localized prosodic manipulations slightly reduce speaker similarity, indicating a tradeoff between expressiveness and timbre consistency.
The approach relies on a large-scale annotated dataset, which may limit applicability in low-resource languages or domains without such data.
No explicit mechanistic or theoretical modeling beyond architectural design and loss functions is provided.
open_questions: How can tone control be further disentangled from other acoustic attributes to achieve fully independent manipulation?
Can the WordVoice framework be adapted or extended to low-resource languages lacking large-scale annotated datasets?
What are the impacts of explicit multi-dimensional control on downstream tasks such as emotion recognition or speaker adaptation?
How does the tradeoff between localized prosodic expressiveness and speaker similarity affect user acceptance in real-world applications?

papers.title: Knowledgeless Language Models: Suppressing Parametric Recall for Evidence-Grounded Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Language models encode substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, which can lead to unreliable behavior when this knowledge is outdated, incomplete, or misaligned with the provided context. In this work, we study whether modifying the pretraining signal can systematically shift models away from parametric recall and toward evidence-grounded reasoning. We introduce Knowledge--''Less'' Language Models (KLLMs), a fundamentally different epistemic training paradigm for LLMs, which are pretrained on corpora in which named entities are anonymized, thereby removing a primary channel for entity-linked factual supervision. This intervention substantially reduces closed-book factual recall, while often improving performance on tasks where relevant information is provided as context. Across multiple model scales, KLLMs consistently outperform matched baselines on contextual question answering, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks. Crucially, in retrieval-grounded settings with imperfect evidence, KLLMs show improved robustness and achieve up to 20--25\% relative gains over standard language models. They further exhibit better calibration, with improved ECE, Brier score, and AUROC, as well as more reliable abstention behavior. Our results demonstrate that suppressing entity-linked supervision during pretraining induces a shift in epistemic behavior: KLLMs rely less on parametric knowledge and more on external evidence, leading to improved reliability under realistic conditions. This suggests that pretraining-time control over knowledge acquisition can complement retrieval-augmented and tool-based systems by providing a more evidence-sensitive base model.

summary.takeaway: Pretraining language models on anonymized corpora reduces parametric factual recall and improves evidence-grounded reasoning, robustness, and calibration.
summary.problem: Language models rely heavily on parametric knowledge, which can be outdated or misaligned, causing unreliable behavior in evidence-grounded tasks.
summary.method: KLLMs are pretrained on corpora with anonymized named entities to suppress entity-linked factual supervision and shift models toward external evidence reliance.
summary.evidence: KLLMs outperform matched baselines by up to 20–25% on retrieval-grounded tasks with imperfect evidence and show improved calibration metrics like ECE, Brier score, and AUROC.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed quantitative results or ablation studies on the impact of anonymization granularity or downstream task diversity.
summary.why_for_you: This approach offers a novel pretraining paradigm to enhance trustworthy LLM behavior by reducing harmful parametric recall and improving robustness in evidence-grounded applications.

signals.text: KLLMs pretrained on anonymized corpora reduce closed-book factual recall but improve performance on contextual QA, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks.
The anonymization of named entities during pretraining removes a primary channel for entity-linked factual supervision, fundamentally shifting the epistemic behavior of LLMs.
In retrieval-grounded settings with imperfect evidence, KLLMs achieve up to 20–25% relative gains over standard LMs and exhibit better calibration metrics such as ECE, Brier score, and AUROC.

papers.title: Verifier-Based Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Reasoning Models for Thermal Energy Storage Control
papers.abstract: Buildings are expected to shift cooling loads in response to grid conditions. Thermal energy storage (TES) enables this shift, but scheduling it well requires planning hours ahead under storage constraints. Model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning are difficult to scale across buildings. This study instead adapts an open-weight reasoning model through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We convert exact offline dynamic-programming (DP) action values into dense rewards for every candidate action. Using only 30 training prompts, reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) trains the model as an upper-level scheduler that outputs hourly heat-pump setpoints from text-based states and forecasts. Evaluation uses a deliberately simple office-building TES benchmark where exact DP is tractable and the optimum is known. RFT reduces the open-weight model's emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, close to the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2. GPT-5 nearly matches DP and MPC without task-specific training, while GPT-4o, a non-reasoning LLM, produces higher emissions than the no-storage baseline, so inference-time reasoning appears important. Trace analysis shows that RFT mainly stabilizes observable planning patterns (candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking) rather than creating a new strategy. Robustness and generalization tests clarify what transfers: the reinforced planning patterns persist under forecast errors and an unseen TES condition and carry over to a battery task, but its different structure limits the gains. DP-based verifiable rewards offer a practical way to adapt open-weight reasoning models to building storage scheduling. These results motivate higher-fidelity tests of whole-building control and scalable verifiers for city-scale energy management.

summary.takeaway: Reinforcement fine-tuning with dynamic programming-based verifiable rewards effectively adapts open-weight reasoning models for thermal energy storage scheduling, achieving near-optimal emissions reduction.
summary.problem: Efficiently scheduling thermal energy storage in buildings requires scalable planning under storage constraints, which is challenging for model predictive control and reinforcement learning methods.
summary.method: The study uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards derived from exact offline dynamic programming action values to fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model as an upper-level scheduler.
summary.evidence: Reinforcement fine-tuning reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, closely approaching the dynamic programming optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2 on a simple TES benchmark.
summary.limitations: The approach’s gains are limited when transferring to structurally different tasks like battery control, and higher-fidelity tests on whole-building control remain to be conducted.
summary.why_for_you: This work demonstrates a practical method to leverage verifiable rewards for efficient adversarial training of reasoning LLMs in energy management, relevant for trustworthy and scalable LLM control applications.

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Reliable Rubrics? A Meta-Evaluation for Experiment Reproduction
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is a promising approach for assessing open-ended outputs from LLM-based research agents, particularly in paper reproduction, where direct paper-to-repository comparison is prone to hallucination. However, constructing paper-specific rubrics requires substantial expert effort, limiting the scalability of benchmarks such as PaperBench. In this work, we present, to our knowledge, the first systematic meta-evaluation of LLM-generated rubrics for paper reproduction. We reformulate rubrics into a checklist-style format and evaluate four generation settings across two backbone models. We meta-evaluate generated rubrics intrinsically by semantic similarity and extrinsically by score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Our results show that the augmented settings substantially improves downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching the human baseline, while intrinsic gains are more modest. Further analyses reveal that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to paper domains, highlighting both the affordances and limitations.

summary.takeaway: Augmented LLM-generated rubrics substantially improve alignment with human evaluation in paper reproduction tasks, nearing human baseline performance.
summary.problem: Constructing paper-specific rubrics for evaluating LLM-based paper reproduction is expert-intensive and limits benchmark scalability.
summary.method: The study meta-evaluates LLM-generated rubrics reformulated into checklist format across four generation settings and two backbone models using intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment.
summary.evidence: Augmented rubric generation settings show substantial improvement in downstream evaluation alignment, with the best setting approaching human baseline, despite modest intrinsic semantic gains.
summary.limitations: LLM-generated rubrics tend to be overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to diverse paper domains.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides critical insights into automating rubric generation for trustworthy evaluation of LLM research agents, addressing hallucination-prone direct comparisons.

signals.text: The strongest augmented rubric generation setting achieves downstream evaluation alignment close to human baseline, demonstrating effective rubric automation for paper reproduction.
Rubrics are reformulated into a checklist-style format and evaluated across four generation settings and two backbone LLMs, enabling systematic meta-evaluation of rubric quality.
Intrinsic evaluation via semantic similarity shows only modest gains, indicating that semantic closeness alone is insufficient to guarantee evaluation alignment.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of scalable, reliable evaluation of LLM-generated research outputs in paper reproduction tasks, where direct comparison to repositories is prone to hallucination. The authors propose automating rubric generation using LLMs and conduct the first systematic meta-evaluation of these rubrics. They convert rubrics into checklist-style formats and test four generation settings across two backbone models. Evaluation is twofold: intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Results reveal that augmented rubric generation settings significantly improve downstream evaluation alignment, nearly matching human baselines, while intrinsic semantic similarity gains remain modest. Further analysis uncovers that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly detailed, biased toward higher scores, and less adaptable across paper domains. These findings highlight both the potential and current limitations of LLM-generated rubrics for trustworthy, scalable evaluation in LLM-based research agent benchmarks.

papers.title: Proxy Exploration and Reusable Guidance: A Modular LLM Post-Training Paradigm via Proxy-Guided Update Signals
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for refining the domain-specific capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet existing reward optimization and distribution matching methods tightly couple policy exploration with distribution alignment. This coupling forces expensive exploration directly on the policy model and severely hinders the asynchronous generation, reuse, and cross-model transfer of optimization signals. In this paper, we propose Proxy-guided Update Signal Transfer (PUST), a novel post-training framework that fundamentally decouples update-signal exploration from distribution alignment. Instead of utilizing the primary model for costly exploration, PUST employs a lightweight proxy model as an efficient testbed to discover high-reward behaviors. We extract the relative improvement signal between the proxy's initial and optimized states, transferring this directional update to the primary model to guide its policy alignment. This decoupled pipeline, comprising proxy exploration, update-signal extraction, and signal transfer, significantly reduces computational overhead and enables optimization signals to be asynchronously generated, cached, and reused. Crucially, by transferring relative improvements rather than absolute policy distributions, PUST naturally supports weak-to-strong improvement and seamless cross-model transfer. Systematic evaluations on Qwen3-family models across math and code domains demonstrate that update signals extracted from substantially weaker proxies can robustly and adjustably enhance stronger primary models. Ultimately, PUST transforms post-training from a monolithic online optimization process into a highly modular, reusable, and cost-efficient paradigm.

papers.title: Estimating Uncertainty from Reasoning: A Large-Scale Study of Multi- and Crosslingual MCQA Performance in LLMs
papers.abstract: Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables LLM-powered systems to recognize when to abstain, yet existing research has predominantly focused on English. We present the first large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages, spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource settings. Using two human-curated Q\&A datasets, we compare open and closed box UE methods (nine in total) across different model sizes and architectures while eliciting long-form reasoning, avoiding LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring, which can introduce evaluation noise. We report three main actionable findings. First, we find that prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, suggesting that comprehension of low-resource languages is largely intact, and that the reliability bottleneck lies in generation rather than understanding. Second, prompting models to reason in English closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages, demonstrating that generation language matters more than the question language. Third, the choice of UE method should depend on model scale: at smaller scales, open-box probability-based methods outperform alternatives; at larger scales, closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty becomes superior. Finally, we provide an analysis of threshold selection for selective prediction, offering guidance on calibrating abstention in multilingual settings.

The closed-box Self Verbalized method achieves an average AUROC of 0.72, outperforming other methods, particularly in high-resource languages.
